questions.q: What is 'zero trust theater,' as defined in this lesson?
options: Any zero trust initiative that costs more than its original budget
An implementation that produces the appearance of a control — a purchased product, a checked compliance box — without reducing implicit trust or real risk
A training exercise where security staff role-play an incident
A product that is marketed under a name other than 'zero trust'
questions.explain: Theater is the gap between appearing to implement zero trust and actually producing less implicit trust and a smaller blast radius.

questions.q: Why does allow-listing every existing access path when deploying a new control count as a sign of theater?
options: Because allow-lists are always a security violation by definition
Because it is more expensive than blocking access directly
Because it can make the net effect on real access close to zero, even though the compliance questionnaire can now be answered 'yes'
Because allow-lists require a separate vendor contract
questions.explain: Exempting every existing access path to avoid breaking anything can leave real access almost unchanged, even while the organization can now truthfully claim the control exists.

questions.q: What is the risk of leaving a policy permanently in 'report-only' or 'audit' mode?
options: It logs violations without ever blocking anything, so the control never actually changes what's possible, often to avoid an outage no one wants to own
It automatically escalates to full enforcement after 90 days with no further action needed
It is only available for cloud-native applications
It doubles the licensing cost of the underlying product
questions.explain: A policy stuck in report-only mode can sit there indefinitely, logging what it would have blocked, without ever actually changing what an attacker or user can do.

questions.q: According to this lesson, when is a roadmap item actually 'done'?
options: When the project plan marks it as shipped
When the vendor confirms the license is active
When the compliance questionnaire can be answered 'yes'
When there is a measurable before/after showing less implicit trust and a smaller blast radius, not just that it shipped
questions.explain: The lesson's core test is a before/after comparison of real access, not a shipped/not-shipped checkbox or a compliance answer.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is the right way to prove an initiative like micro-segmentation worked?
options: Citing the vendor's published case studies
Showing a concrete before/after, such as a specific compromised account reaching 40 systems before rollout and 3 systems after, with the same privileges
Counting the number of policies written, regardless of enforcement state
Reporting the dollar amount spent on the initiative
questions.explain: Only a concrete before/after access comparison, not a policy count or a spend figure, demonstrates that the control actually changed what's reachable.
